content:
An NGO's annual report and audited financial statements belong on one clearly labelled page of the website, with each year's documents as separate, plainly named files, a short readable summary in ordinary web text beside each PDF, and a note of what the figures cover. Donors, CSR teams and funders look for this page before they give, and a page that is easy to find and easy to read says more about an organisation than any claim on the home page. If you are commissioning NGO website development in India, specify this page at the start, because getting the structure right is far easier than untangling a folder of files called "final_v3_new.pdf" later.

This guide is for NGO leaders, communications staff and the developers who build their sites. It covers what to publish, how to organise it, how to prepare PDFs so they are readable, accessible and findable, what to say in a web summary without overstating anything, and how to keep the page current. It does not say what you are legally required to publish. That depends on your registration, your funding and your state, and it should be confirmed with your chartered accountant. Where we mention obligations, we say so and point you to your adviser.

## Why This Page Matters to Donors and Funders

People who are about to give money, whether Rs 500 or a CSR grant, look for evidence that the organisation is real, accountable and careful. The financial documents are that evidence. A CSR team doing due diligence will usually ask for registration certificates, audited statements and an annual report; a donor with less time will simply look for them on your site and draw a conclusion if they are missing.

A good page does three things. It answers "can I trust you with money?" before anyone has to ask. It saves your team the time of emailing the same documents again and again. And it gives search engines a stable, descriptive place to find your reporting, which helps people who search for your organisation's name together with words like "annual report" or "audited accounts".

Our broader guides on [transparency and impact reporting for NGO websites](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-transparency-impact-reporting-2026) and the [NGO donation transparency checklist](/blog/ngo-donation-transparency-checklist) describe what a trustworthy site shows. This article focuses on the practical build of the reporting page itself.

## What to Publish

Start with what you have. Many organisations hold more reportable material than they realise.

### Core documents

- **Annual report** for each financial year: the narrative of what you did, with numbers, photographs and stories.
- **Audited financial statements** for each year, including the balance sheet, income and expenditure account and the auditor's report.
- **Registration and recognition documents** you are comfortable sharing publicly, such as the trust deed or registration certificate and tax-exemption certificates. Confirm with your adviser which documents should be public and which should be shared on request.

### Optional but valuable

- **Programme or impact reports** for specific projects or funders.
- **A governance page** listing trustees or board members and key policies. See our guide on [navigation that serves donors, volunteers and CSR partners](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-navigation-menu-donors-volunteers-csr-partners-2026) for where it should sit in your menu.
- **A plain-language summary** of how funds were used.

### What not to publish

Do not publish documents that contain personal data of beneficiaries, donors or staff, such as bank account numbers, PAN numbers of individuals, home addresses or case files. Review each PDF before upload and, if necessary, redact it properly, which means removing the text, not drawing a black box over it that can be lifted. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, organisations that handle personal data have responsibilities, and our guide to [donor data protection under the DPDP Act](/blog/ngo-donor-data-protection-dpdp-act-2026) explains what to review. Consult your legal adviser about your own position.

## Design the Page Structure

A reporting page is a list of documents, so the design question is how to make the list obvious.

### Use a stable, descriptive URL

Choose an address such as `/reports/` or `/annual-reports/` and keep it forever. If you must change it, redirect the old address. Put the page in the main navigation or the footer under a label people expect, such as "Reports", "Annual reports" or "Financials", not an inventive name like "Our Journey in Numbers".

### One section per financial year, newest first

Group documents by year, with the newest at the top. Under each year, list the annual report and the audited statements as two clearly labelled links. Indian financial years run from April to March, so label them "FY 2024-25 (April 2024 to March 2025)" rather than just "2025", which is ambiguous.

### Label each link so it makes sense alone

A link that says "Click here" or "Download" tells a screen-reader user, and Google, nothing. Write the link text as a full description: "Annual Report 2024-25 (PDF, 3.2 MB)" or "Audited Financial Statements 2024-25 (PDF, 1.1 MB)". Giving the file type and size lets people on slow mobile connections decide before tapping. This follows the W3C guidance that link text should describe its purpose ([W3C WCAG 2.2: Link Purpose](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/link-purpose-in-context.html)).

### Add a short summary in HTML

Beside each year, add three to six lines of ordinary text: total income, total expenditure and the main purposes of spending, copied accurately from the audited statements. Visitors who just want a quick answer will not open a PDF, and text on the page is easier to read on a phone, easier for search engines to understand and easier for assistive technology.

Only publish numbers you can match to the documents. If a figure is not in the audited statements, do not put it in a summary. If you describe how funds were used in percentages, make sure the categories match your statements. Never write "100% of your donation goes to the cause" unless your accountant confirms that statement is accurate for your accounts and you explain what it includes.

## Prepare the PDFs Properly

A PDF is a document format, not a web page, and a careless export produces files that are huge, unreadable on phones, inaccessible and unfindable. A short checklist fixes most of it.

### Name the files descriptively

Use names like `exampleNGO-annual-report-2024-25.pdf`, in lower case with hyphens. File names appear in search results and downloads, and a descriptive name helps both people and search engines.

### Keep the file size reasonable

A 40 MB report full of uncompressed photographs is a poor experience on mobile data. Export from your design software with image compression, and aim to keep the main annual report to a size most phones can open comfortably. Provide a link to a smaller text-focused version if the design version is large. If your report is a magazine-style design file, consider offering a lighter version of the same content.

### Make the PDF accessible

Accessibility matters for visitors with visual impairments and for anyone using a screen reader. The W3C publishes techniques for making PDFs accessible, including real headings, text that can be selected (not scanned images), descriptive alternative text for images, a defined document language and a logical reading order ([W3C: PDF techniques for WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Techniques/#pdf)). In practice:

1. **Use real text.** A scanned stack of paper pages is a set of pictures. Where you must publish a scan, run optical character recognition so the text can be read, then check the result.
2. **Use heading styles** in the source document (Word, InDesign) before exporting, so the PDF carries a structure.
3. **Add alternative text** to images that carry meaning, and mark decorative images as such.
4. **Set the document title and language** in the PDF properties.
5. **Check tables.** Financial statements are tables, and a table that is an image or has no header row is unusable for a screen reader.
6. **Run an accessibility checker** built into your PDF software and fix what it reports.

India's guidelines for government websites and the broader accessibility standards for Indian sites are discussed in our [WCAG accessibility checklist for Indian websites](/blog/wcag-accessibility-checklist-india). A non-profit is not a government site, but the same practices serve your visitors.

### Can Google find your PDFs?

Google can index PDF files and show them in search results, as long as they are crawlable and contain text ([Google Search Central: file types Google can index](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/indexable-file-types)). Do not block your reports folder in `robots.txt`, and do not hide the page behind a login or a form. If the report is confidential, keep it off the website entirely. If it is meant to be public, make sure the page that links to it is crawlable and listed in your XML sitemap.

### Do not rely on PDFs alone

Where your annual report has stories and findings you want people to read, publish the key parts as ordinary web pages as well, and link to the PDF for the full version. Web pages load faster, can be linked to precisely, work better on phones and are easier to keep up to date. Our guide to [beneficiary stories, photographs and consent](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-beneficiary-stories-photos-consent-2026) explains how to publish stories ethically.

## Version Control and Keeping the Page Current

An out-of-date reporting page is worse than a short one, because it suggests the organisation has gone quiet. Build a few habits.

- **Assign an owner** for the page, with a named backup.
- **Set a reminder** shortly after your auditor signs off each year, so the new documents go up promptly and the old ones stay in the archive.
- **Keep older years** in an archive section; do not delete them. Donors and funders compare years.
- **Never replace a published file silently.** If you must correct a document, note on the page that it was corrected and when. Keep the earlier version only if your adviser says it is appropriate.
- **Date the page.** Show "Last updated: [date]" in plain text, and make sure it is true.
- **Check links twice a year.** A broken download link on a financial page looks careless.

## How the Page Fits Into the Rest of the Site

### Link to it from where trust is decided

Link to the reports page from the donation page, the footer, the About section and any CSR partnership page. A donor on the donation form who wonders "where does the money go?" should be one click from the answer. Our guide on [donation page design](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-page-design-2026) shows how to place such trust information next to the donate button without cluttering it.

### Use the page in outreach

When you reply to a CSR enquiry or a funder's request for documents, send the link to your reports page first. It is also a tidy resource to attach to grant applications, since it shows the documents are public and consistent.

### Keep the organisation's details consistent

The name, registration details and address in your reports should match what appears in the website footer and on any public profile, such as a Google Business Profile. Our guide on [setting up a Google Business Profile for an NGO centre](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-google-business-profile-local-search-2026) covers keeping that consistent.

## A Worked Example of a Reports Page

Here is an illustrative layout for a fictional organisation, to show the structure. It is not a real client page.

**Reports and financials** (page title)

*Intro:* "Every year our accounts are audited by an independent chartered accountant. Our reports are below. If you need an older document or have a question, write to accounts@example.org." *Last updated: [date].*

**FY 2024-25 (April 2024 to March 2025)**
- Annual Report 2024-25 (PDF, 3.2 MB)
- Audited Financial Statements 2024-25 (PDF, 1.1 MB)
- Summary: Income Rs [amount]; expenditure Rs [amount]; main areas of spending: [list from the statements].

**FY 2023-24**
- Annual Report 2023-24 (PDF, [size])
- Audited Financial Statements 2023-24 (PDF, [size])

**Registrations and policies**
- Registration certificate (PDF)
- [Other documents your adviser approves]

Every bracket is a place for real data from your own accounts. Do not fill brackets with estimates.

## Common Mistakes

1. **Hiding the page** in a footer link with an obscure label.
2. **Publishing scans** that cannot be searched, read aloud or opened easily on phones.
3. **Uploading documents with personal data** that was never meant to be public.
4. **Listing summary figures that do not match the audited statements.**
5. **Using vague filenames** and no year labels.
6. **Letting the page go stale** after one upload.
7. **Making visitors fill in a form** to see public documents, which looks as though you have something to hide.

## Questions Donors and CSR Teams Commonly Ask

It helps to read your page as a stranger would. In our experience of building reporting sections for non-profits, the questions that come up repeatedly are practical ones, and a good page answers them without being asked.

- **Is the organisation registered, and under what?** Show the type of registration and the registered name exactly as it appears on documents.
- **Who audits the accounts?** Name the audit firm if your adviser is comfortable with that, and state the financial year covered.
- **How much was spent on programmes and how much on administration?** Only answer this if your statements support the categories, and say how you define each one.
- **Where does funding come from?** A simple breakdown of the main sources, if you can share it, builds confidence.
- **Who can I contact about the accounts?** A named person and an email address, monitored by someone who will actually reply.

If you cannot answer one of these on the page, decide deliberately whether to publish it later or to explain how a donor can request it. Silence reads as avoidance, while an honest "available on request" does not.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What financial documents should an NGO publish on its website?
Commonly the annual report and audited financial statements for each year, plus registration and recognition certificates you are comfortable making public. What you are required to publish depends on your registration and funders, so confirm it with your chartered accountant.

### Should an NGO publish its audited accounts as PDF or on a web page?
Both. Keep the signed audited statements as a PDF, because that is the formal document, and add a short summary on a web page so that visitors can read the key facts quickly and search engines can understand them.

### How can I make an annual report PDF accessible?
Use real text rather than scanned images, apply heading styles before exporting, add alternative text to meaningful images, set the document language and title, check that tables have header rows, and run the accessibility checker in your PDF software.

### Will Google index my NGO's annual report PDF?
Google can index PDF files that are crawlable and contain readable text. Do not block them in robots.txt or place them behind a login, and link to them from a crawlable page listed in your sitemap.

### How often should an NGO update its reports page?
At least once a year after the audit is complete, and whenever you publish a new report or correct a document. Show the date of the last update on the page and review links twice a year.
